newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Mature chemical industry eyes brighter 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mature chemical industry eyes brighter 1997.

text.p: -The mature chemical industries of western Europe and the United States are looking forward to a brighter 1997 but need to work hard to meet growing Asian competition, industry leaders said on Thursday.

ICI Plc chief economist Richard Freeman predicted that output from western Europe's chemical industry would expand by 3.3 percent this year after a sluggish one percent gain in 1996, driven by faster economic growth, rising exports and low chemical stocks.

But he warned that the days when the industry's growth rates traditionally outstripped expansion in GDP are rapidly coming to an end in Europe and the U.S, "in marked contrast to the dynamic picture of the chemical industry in Asia, which is attracting increasing inward investment."

Freeman told the 12th business outlook conference of Britain's Chemical Industries Association (CIA) that 1997 "is shaping up to be a fairly good year for the industry in western Europe," the world's biggest chemicals producer.
The year's best performer is likely to be Germany which Freeman predicted would see production rise by 4 percent in volume terms as it recovered from a slide of 0.6 percent in 1996.

In Frankfurt, Juergen Strube, head of the German chemical industry group VCI said on Thursday that a turnaround for Germany's chemical companies is on the cards for 1997, despite a two percent fall in turnover in 1996.
"Most of our members expect a somewhat more favourable development of the economy for 1997 than in the previous year and corresponding growth," said Strube, who is also chief executive of BASF AG.

Britain, which the CIA expects to enjoy the largest GDP growth of any major European economy this year, should see volumes rise by nearly 3.0 percent after a gain of 2.1 percent last year. And France is tipped to see a second year of solid expansion, rising 3.0 percent this year after a 2.8 percent increase last year.

Prospects in the mighty U.S. industry are even brighter. Fred Webber, President of the U.S. Chemical Manufacturers Association, predicted a 4.4 percent rise in the sales of companies with annual turnover in excess of $1 billion, and 5.0 percent for the rest.
He said companies also expected a bumper year for profits as they benefited from an easing of raw material prices and other cost pressures.

But as in Europe Webber said the maturing of the U.S. industry meant that "for the foreseeable future, the growth in demand for chemicals, excepting pharmaceuticals, will be slow relative to growth in GDP."

He blamed the relative decline on the shift of the U.S. economy towards the service sector, which used fewer chemical products than traditional customers like manufacturing, construction and other heavy industries. Webber said demand for new housing appeared to have peaked from its highs in the 1970s, while growth of another key chemical user, the car industry, was likely to show "only modest trend growth."
U.S. companies, Webber said, would be forced to increase exports and invest in developing markets, many of which "have chemical needs that expand at twice the rate of economic growth."
"The export markets of the future are...in fast-growing developing countries, particularly in Asia and Latin America," he told the conference.

Underlining the opportunities, ICI India managing director Aditya Narayan said India was expected to emerge as the world's fourth-largest economy over the next two decades, trailing another awakening giant, China.

For the British chemical industry, which is currently Europe's third largest with annual sales of around 40 billion pounds, CIA director general Elliot Finer said research and new product innovation were crucial to future success.
